_comment: Mutation testing answers the one question the review rounds kept asking by hand: if this guard were removed, would anything notice? Three findings in a row came from deleting a check and watching the suite stay green, and the first full run found three more. Concurrency is cores minus two; four left seven of ten idle.
runner_comment: Not `npm test`: that also runs test/hygiene.test.mjs, which reads the tracked files looking for real personal data. A mutant in index.js cannot change what is written in a file, so those 10.7 seconds were spent 832 times to learn nothing. The two files left are the ones that drive index.js. If a mutant ever survives that only hygiene would have caught, this line is the reason, and hygiene still runs on every commit.
incremental_comment: Off, and it has to be. Incremental reuse is decided per mutant from which tests covered and killed it — and the command runner reports the whole suite as ONE synthetic test, whose identity does not change when a test file does. So every mutant looks reusable after any test change, and a run that should have re-checked the new tests reports the old numbers instead. That happened here: an edited config gave an identical 832-NoCoverage summary in twelve seconds. Turning it on again needs coverageAnalysis, which needs a runner that loads the code in-process, which this suite cannot use because it drives the server over stdio as a child.
timeout_comment: Both of these were tuned once in the wrong direction, and the way that showed is worth keeping: at concurrency 12 on a 10-core machine with timeoutMS 10000, the score went from 76.92% to 89.66% and the timeout count went from 172 to 531. Nothing got better. Stryker counts a timeout as detected, which scores exactly like a kill, so a mutant whose run is merely slow is recorded as caught — and 12 runners on 10 cores make every run slow, while the allowance is computed from a netTime measured on an idle machine. The two settings fought each other and the score inflated. So: concurrency at cores minus two, and an allowance of timeoutFactor * netTime + timeoutMS + measured overhead that leaves a mutant well over half a minute. The number to watch when changing either is not the score, it is the timeout count — if it climbs, the score is being manufactured.
